deep.reconstruction:
Setting (pp. 13–15 of this series, archive pp. 56–58). Grothendieck is listing the elementary operations on 'decomposed' oriented topological surfaces. These operations are meant to generate the morphisms of what he calls the topological Teichmüller groupoids (next page: 'traduire les groupoïdes de Teichmüller topologiques'). The data on a surface are as follows.
- A system Σ_0 of disjoint cut circles (a pants-type decomposition).
- A dual graph with edge set A_0, together with free edges A_ℓ corresponding to boundary circles.
- Combinatorial 'marking' data R. On p. 13 these are torsors R_a under Z_a/r(a), where Z_a = Z_{±1} ∧ ω(a) is an orientation twist. They play the role of level structures or basepoints on circles.
- Σ^+ ⊂ Σ_0 is the set of marked circles.

The previous page treated 'géométrie partielle' and 'sous-géométrie uniforme'. These restrict or extend the structure groups Z/r(a) → Z/r'(a) or Z/r''(a), with multiplier d(a). Operation B (inferred) was 'gommer': erase a cut circle, i.e. contract an edge of the dual graph.

This page is operation C), découpage (cutting).
- Choose a subset Σ' ⊂ Σ_0 of cut circles, equivalently a subset A' ⊂ A_0 of internal edges.
- Instead of erasing these circles, cut the surface along them.
- On the dual graph, each edge of A' is cut at its midpoint and replaced by two free edges (two new boundary components).

He then separates two cases.
- The 'ordinary' case: the cut circle C is marked, i.e. C ∩ R ≠ ∅, i.e. C ⊂ Σ^+. The marking then transfers to both new boundary circles. The parenthetical says that, apart from this, an ambiguity in some finite case can arise, apparently resolved with the help of data produced by the operation.
- The case where C is not marked. Here the new boundary circles carry no basepoint or level data.

He remarks that in the intended framework only effectively marked circles will occur. On the next page he adds that one may still 'gommer' (forget) the markings midway.

The next page introduces D), recollement (gluing), as the essential inverse operation. Its data are a fixed-point-free involution on a subset of free edges, plus orientation-reversing identifications of the paired boundary circles.

In modern terms, these are the cutting and gluing (and edge-contraction) operations on stable graphs and marked surfaces. They underlie the Teichmüller tower of the Esquisse, the Moore–Seiberg / Bakalov–Kirillov 'Lego' presentation of mapping class groupoids, and modular operads.
errors: No mathematical error. The treatment of the unmarked case is left incomplete: he only notes that it will not arise in practice. The parenthetical about a possible ambiguity 'in a finite case' is too illegible to evaluate.

ideas.what: Cutting a decomposed surface along a subset of its decomposition circles; on the dual graph, cutting an edge at its midpoint into two free half-edges
ideas.modern_name: Cutting operation on stable graphs / boundary maps of moduli spaces; modular operad structure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore in Deligne–Mumford–Knudsen boundary theory; formalised by Getzler–Kapranov (modular operads, 1998); Moore–Seiberg (1989); Bakalov–Kirillov (2000)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984), §3 on the Teichmüller tower and the 'Lego-Teichmüller' game (cutting/gluing of surfaces), stated less formally

ideas.what: Distinguishing marked circles (C ∩ R ≠ ∅, C ⊂ Σ^+) from unmarked ones when cutting, so that basepoints or level torsors propagate to the new boundary components
ideas.modern_name: Surfaces with marked points / tangential basepoints on boundary circles; framed or level-structured boundary
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Hatcher–Lochak–Schneps, Moore–Seiberg and Bakalov–Kirillov treatments of boundary parametrisations

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine step in Grothendieck's systematic enumeration of operations (contract, cut, glue) on decomposed surfaces and their dual graphs. The ideas match the cut-and-paste formalism later standard in the Teichmüller tower / Lego literature and in modular operads, and they are sketched in the Esquisse. Nothing on this page goes beyond that.
